final_proof:
Assume, as is standard in this problem, that \(\mathbb N=\{1,2,3,\ldots\}\). The asserted claim is not currently a proved theorem: after putting \(m=k+1\), the equation becomes
\[
1^p+2^p+\cdots +(m-1)^p=m^p,
\]
which is precisely the Erdős–Moser equation, and the assertion that its only positive-integer solution is \((m,p)=(3,1)\) is the Erdős–Moser conjecture. Thus one cannot at present give a rigorous unconditional proof of the stated claim. What can be proved elementarily—and in particular shows exactly why only even exponents remain open—is the following corrected theorem.

**Corrected theorem.** Among positive-integer solutions for which \(p\) is odd, the unique solution is \((k,p)=(2,1)\). Consequently, every hypothetical additional positive-integer solution must have even exponent \(p\).

**Proof.** Suppose that \(p\) is odd and that
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{k}j^p=(k+1)^p.\tag{1}
\]
The case \(k=1\) is impossible, since (1) would say \(1=2^p\). Hence \(k\ge 2\). Reduce (1) modulo \(k\). The term \(k^p\) vanishes, while \((k+1)^p\equiv 1\pmod{k}\), so
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}j^p\equiv 1\pmod{k}.\tag{2}
\]
If \(k\) is odd, the integers \(1,\ldots,k-1\) split into disjoint pairs \(\{j,k-j\}\). Because \(p\) is odd, each pair satisfies
\[
j^p+(k-j)^p\equiv j^p+(-j)^p=0\pmod{k}.
\]
Thus the left-hand side of (2) is congruent to \(0\pmod{k}\), contradicting (2). Therefore \(k\) is even.

Write \(k=2a\). Pairing \(j\) with \(k-j\) as above now cancels every term in the sum in (2) except the unpaired middle term \(j=k/2=a\). Hence (2) gives
\[
a^p\equiv 1\pmod{2a}.
\]
In particular, \(a\mid a^p-1\). But also \(a\mid a^p\), since \(p\ge1\); subtracting shows that \(a\mid1\). As \(a\) is positive, \(a=1\), and therefore \(k=2\). Equation (1) is then
\[
1+2^p=3^p.\tag{3}
\]
For \(p=1\), (3) holds. For every \(p>1\), the factorization
\[
3^p-2^p=(3-2)\bigl(3^{p-1}+3^{p-2}2+\cdots+2^{p-1}\bigr)>1
\]
shows that \(3^p\ne2^p+1\). Thus \(p=1\), proving the corrected theorem. \(\square\)

If instead one uses the convention \(0\in\mathbb N\), the original assertion is additionally false on its face: \((k,p)=(1,0)\) satisfies the equation (all bases involved are positive). The standard positive-integer convention avoids this extra solution but leaves the even-exponent Erdős–Moser conjecture unresolved.
